chapter: First bands, Ennis, Thornhill and the Army
title: Realising band members had African ancestry; no Black people in Stockton
summary: Gil reflects that several early bandmates had African ancestry he never noticed. He says he knew no Black friends until New York. Transcriber notes are interleaved.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: At times we did. We had a fellow named Alex Davis who was a vocalist with us for a while. And he went to Lake Tahoe with us. You see, I really didn't know anything in those days about the sociology of people or anything like that. Since then sometimes I've talked to Anita about it because it turns out that so many of those men, now I realise, whose parents somewhere were from Africa.
You know, they had African in them. But they were all, you know Irish. Ned Riggs brother for example, he had a rather classic African head. You know, the narrow kind of shape like that.
And the whole thing, his name was

Clark Briggs, huh? His mother was from the South. I remember it, and now I look back and see some of those people, for example, Herb Stowe, (the guy I was telling you was the grandson of Harriet Beecher Stowe), his mother, I realise now, was really, had lots of you know African (blood, has to?). She was a very handsome woman.

But I never even, you know I never even thought about that at the time in those days because there were, actually there were no black people at all over in Stockton. None. And none where I most of the people lived in Norwich. There were people like Swedes, you know, in mining country it was all full of Swedes.
And out of Stockton, the people that got picked on there were Philippino. So I really didn't have any Afro-American friends, you know, until I moved to New York, really.

It's funny, all of a sudden all of my friends were, the whole thing turned out........ But that was just never part of my, I never thought of it you know. But later, and looking back now I could see how some of those people were, must have been terrified they were going to be

Yes, yes, they're out there passing, right? Yes, and especially on the Coast where you did have all of these people of varying colors, they could get by with it. Yes. Because I'm sure you saw Filipinos darker than some of the people who had that African blood.

I had a Filipino taxi driver on the Islands when we were on a sightseeing tour and he was talking in the front seat, I was in the back seat. He sounded exactly like Ainto who was a Brazilian percussionist. He's down at the concert that day. He was one of the percussionists, and Ainto is from Brazil and he has a certain accent when he speaks English. This man had the identical accent.
